- position limit 10

- buy order of 9, sell order of 9

oat is more right on the actual technical point.
Why: the smoothness of an equity curve does not tell you whether a strategy is overfit. Smooth ≠ robust, and jagged ≠ not overfit.
deltasigma’s main mistake: treating “my graph isn’t perfectly smooth” as evidence against overfitting. That logic just does not hold.
What is true in deltasigma’s favor: a suspiciously perfect, monotonic, “too good to be true” curve can be a red flag for hardcoding/leakage/exploiting the simulator. But it is only a red flag, not proof.
Bottom line: oat’s claim is better because he says graph smoothness is not an indicator either way, which is much closer to correct.

The core issue is that overfitting is about whether the strategy has learned real structure or just fit noise / specific quirks of the sample environment. A curve’s appearance is, at best, a weak hint.

Why deltasigma’s argument fails:

You can have a noisy overfit strategy.
Example: you tune a bunch of parameters until they happen to work on the tutorial data. The result may still have drawdowns and jaggedness. It is still overfit if it collapses out of sample.
You can have a smooth non-overfit strategy.
A simple, genuine edge can produce a pretty smooth curve if the environment is favorable.
You can also have a smooth overfit strategy.
Especially if there is leakage, hardcoding, or a deterministic exploitable pattern in the simulator.

So the statement “my graph is not smooth, therefore I can’t be overfit” is wrong. That is exactly what oat was pushing back on.

Where deltasigma is partly right:

If you are extremely close to the theoretical max PnL in a toy environment, and the curve is absurdly clean, then yes, that can make people suspicious of:
hardcoding
future leakage
exploiting a fixed simulator artifact
using overly specific rules that won’t generalize

But again, that is suspicion, not a valid test.

The better way to judge overfitting is:

Does it work on data / periods / scenarios you did not tune on?
Is it stable when you slightly change parameters?
Does the logic make economic / microstructural sense?
Does performance survive after removing one feature / rule?
Is it dependent on some hyper-specific pattern that probably disappears later?

So in that chat:

oat wins the technical argument

The tutorial round is essentially like this.
You upload a trader file, which essentially is the entire code a HFT firm would need.
You have the days -2, -1, but not 0 available. You can research on days -2 and -1. But your code will always be tested on day 0. Like any decent train,test split would
So if you implement code, it is essentially only run on the hidden data for day 0.
When round 1 comes around, you will be able to run training/research on days -1, 0. But your code will be tested on day 1.
and so on.

**⚠️ DO NOT opt into rankings on prosperity.equirag.com**

This is a third-party visualizer (not official IMC). If you enable "Opt Into Rankings" and upload a raw .log file, your **entire log is sent to and stored on their server**. Their own UI says it's retained for "verification, future revalidation, and fraud review."

**What's in your .log file:**
- Every order you placed (prices, volumes, timing)
- Your PnL curve and position at every tick
- Your algorithm's debug prints (fair value estimates, quote prices, signal triggers)
- Your serialized traderData (persisted state between ticks)

Anyone with server access can reverse-engineer your strategy from this.

**Safe usage:** Upload WITHOUT opt-in → data stays in your browser (client-side JS only). Verify by checking your browser's Network tab during upload — no requests should go to their API.

That could also be problematic.

Think of it like using a predefined backtester from your broker or trading software. It’s not bad per se, but there are some risks.

Backtesters from previous editions may have already been analyzed and indirectly taken into account when designing the current market and asset universe.

Also, since many contestants are likely doing the same thing, you could end up with a clustering of very similar strategies and sources of edge, as everyone would essentially be backtesting on the same market, assets, and time series.

Even if your edge doesn’t completely disappear, you might still get “Robinhooded” — or simply outperformed — by other bots exploiting the same signals. Moreover, if the market design deliberately reduces common alpha sources (e.g. strong trends or momentum), and instead emphasizes noise, stochastic behavior, and fat-tailed distributions, those strategies may become even less effective.
Just philosophizing, still being a thing you could do, if not the best thing to do considering the different alternatives.

            # --- CLAUDE-GENERATED VIBE CHECK ---
